results.summary: This Wokwi design counts upwards from 0 to 9 and loops back, driving a 7-segment display through its eight output pins. The documentation states that input switches are connected to the segment display using AND gates, with the lowest input toggling the display, though the description is incomplete and partly garbled. No testing procedure has been written yet, as the how-to-test section is marked as a future addition. The project is a simple educational counter with thin documentation and no external hardware specified.

This work-in-progress Wokwi design slows the 10 kHz clock to a lower frequency and shows a rotation of the outer columns on a 7-segment display. Eight switch inputs are exposed alongside eight segment outputs, and the intended test is simply to observe the 7-segment display. The documentation is incomplete, with the target frequency left as an unspecified placeholder and the title still marked WIP. It requires an external 7-segment display to be useful.

This design implements the TEA (Tiny Encryption Algorithm) block cipher in hardware, encrypting a 64-bit data block with a 128-bit key over 32 rounds using 32-bit modular addition, XOR and shifts. It exposes eight data input pins and eight data output pins, and is tested by following the Tiny Tapeout workshop flow to load key and plaintext and read back the ciphertext. A known reference vector is provided with an all-zero key and plaintext producing ciphertext 0x41EA3A0A_94BAA940. No external hardware is required, and the title is still marked WIP despite the detailed algorithm description.

This design is an eight-bit Johnson counter that requires only a clock to count, with the complement of the last flip-flop fed back to the first flip-flop. Its eight outputs expose the counter state, and testing consists of simply turning the circuit on and observing the outputs. No external hardware is needed. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the design and its operation.

This design adds two 4-bit numbers taken from an 8-bit switch input, with the low four switches forming one operand and the high four forming the other, producing a 5-bit sum on five output pins. It is tested by incrementally flipping the eight switches and verifying that the displayed sum is correct. No external hardware is used. The project is a straightforward educational arithmetic circuit built from four sequentially placed adders.

This design implements a single AND gate with two inputs and one output. It is tested by toggling the two input switches between 0 and 1 and observing the output. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and the project appears to be a basic introductory logic experiment.

This design implements a one-bit full adder that takes inputs a, b and carry-in and produces sum and carry-out outputs. A complete truth table is provided, and testing consists of setting the three inputs and verifying the two outputs match the expected values. No external hardware is needed. The project is a basic educational combinational logic block.

This design is described as a first test of the Wokwi-to-GDS flow, combining one AND gate and one OR gate between the eight switch inputs and a digital clock output. Eight input switches and eight outputs are exposed, but the how-to-test section still contains the placeholder text asking the author to explain usage. No external hardware is listed. The documentation is very thin and the project appears to be an introductory experiment rather than a functional design.

This work-in-progress design converts a number entered on the eight input pins into a seven-segment display pattern on the eight output pins. Only one input at a time is supported, and testing consists of entering a number and observing the corresponding digit. No external hardware is used. The documentation is brief and the project is explicitly marked as work in progress.

This design consists of a clock divider and two gates, with a single gate input pin exposed and a 100 Hz clock. The description says changes should be observed on 7-segment LEDs, though no segment outputs are listed among the pins. The how-to-test section is a single garbled sentence, and the external hardware section still contains the template placeholder text. The documentation is too thin to determine the design's actual function with confidence.
